{{Short description|Ways to represent 3D rotations}}
{{broader|3D rotation group}}
In [[geometry]], there exist various formulations to express a [[rotation (mathematics)|rotation]] in [[three dimensions]] as a mathematical [[transformation (geometry)|transformation]]. In physics, this concept is applied to [[classical mechanics]] where rotational (or angular) [[kinematics]] is the science of [[quantity|quantitative]] description of a purely rotational [[motion (physics)|motion]]. The [[orientation (geometry)|orientation]] of an object at a given instant is described with the same tools, as it is defined as an imaginary rotation from a reference placement in space, rather than an actually observed rotation from a previous placement in space.

According to [[Euler's rotation theorem]], the rotation of a [[rigid body]] (or three-dimensional [[coordinate system]] with a fixed [[origin (mathematics)|origin]]) is described by a single rotation about some axis. Such a rotation may be uniquely described by a minimum of three [[real number|real]] parameters. However, for various reasons, there are several ways to represent it. Many of these representations use more than the necessary minimum of three parameters, although each of them still has only three [[degrees of freedom (mechanics)|degrees of freedom]].

An example where rotation representation is used is in [[computer vision]], where an [[automation|automated]] observer needs to track a target. Consider a rigid body, with three [[orthonormal basis|orthogonal unit vectors]]<!-- this kludge works around a sea of blue --> fixed to its body (representing the three axes of the object's local [[Cartesian coordinate system|coordinate system]]). The basic problem is to specify the orientation of these three [[unit vector]]s, and hence the rigid body, with respect to the observer's coordinate system, regarded as a reference placement in space.

==Rotations and motions==
{{main article|Motion (geometry)|Rotation (mathematics)}}
Rotation formulations are focused on proper ([[orientation (vector space)|orientation-preserving]]) motions of the [[Euclidean space]] with [[stabilizer (group theory)|one fixed point]], that a ''rotation'' refers to. Although physical motions with a fixed point are an important case (such as ones described in the [[center-of-mass frame]], or motions of a [[joint (mechanics)|joint]]), this approach creates a knowledge about all motions. Any [[proper motion]] of the Euclidean space decomposes to a rotation around the origin and a [[translation (geometry)|translation]]. Whichever the order of their [[function composition|composition]] will be, the "pure" rotation component wouldn't change, uniquely determined by the complete motion.

One can also understand "pure" rotations as [[linear map]]s in a [[vector space]] equipped with Euclidean structure, not as maps of [[point (geometry)|points]] of a corresponding [[affine space]]. In other words, a rotation formulations captures only the rotational part of a motion, that contains three degrees of freedom, and ignores the translational part, that contains another three.

When representing a rotation as numbers in a computer, some people prefer the quaternion representation or the axis+angle representation, because they avoid the [[gimbal lock]] that can occur with Euler rotations.<ref>
[http://www.questionablyartificial.com/2016---fiducial-marker-tracking-for-augmented-reality.html "Fiducial Marker Tracking for Augmented Reality"].
</ref>

==Alternatives==

===Rotation matrix===
{{Main article|Rotation matrix}}

The above-mentioned triad of [[unit vector]]s is also called a [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]]. Specifying [[real coordinate space|the coordinates]] (''components'') of vectors of this basis in its current (rotated) position, in terms of the reference (non-rotated) coordinate axes, will completely describe the rotation. The three unit vectors, {{math|'''û'''}}, {{math|'''v̂'''}} and {{math|'''ŵ'''}}, that form the rotated basis each consist of 3&nbsp;coordinates, yielding a total of 9&nbsp;parameters.

These parameters can be written as the elements of a {{nowrap|3 × 3}} matrix {{math|'''A'''}}, called a '''rotation matrix'''. Typically, the coordinates of each of these vectors are arranged along a column of the matrix (however, beware that an alternative definition of rotation matrix exists and is widely used, where the vectors' coordinates defined above are arranged by rows<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Rotation Matrix|id=RotationMatrix}}</ref>)
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}
   \hat{\mathbf{u}}_x & \hat{\mathbf{v}}_x & \hat{\mathbf{w}}_x \\
   \hat{\mathbf{u}}_y & \hat{\mathbf{v}}_y & \hat{\mathbf{w}}_y \\
   \hat{\mathbf{u}}_z & \hat{\mathbf{v}}_z & \hat{\mathbf{w}}_z \\
\end{bmatrix}</math>

The elements of the rotation matrix are not all independent—as Euler's rotation theorem dictates, the rotation matrix has only three degrees of freedom.

The rotation matrix has the following properties:
* {{math|'''A'''}} is a real, [[orthogonal matrix]], hence each of its rows or columns represents a [[unit vector]].
* The [[eigenvalue]]s of {{math|'''A'''}} are <math display="block">\left\{1, e^{\pm i\theta} \right\} = \{1,\ \cos\theta+i\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta-i\sin\theta\}</math> where {{math|''i''}} is the standard [[imaginary unit]] with the property {{math|1=''i''<sup>2</sup> = −1}}.
* The [[determinant]] of {{math|'''A'''}} is +1, equivalent to the product of its eigenvalues.
* The [[Trace (linear algebra)|trace]] of {{math|'''A'''}} is {{math|1 + 2 cos ''θ''}}, equivalent to the sum of its eigenvalues.

The angle {{mvar|θ}} which appears in the eigenvalue expression corresponds to the angle of the Euler axis and angle representation. The [[eigenvector]] corresponding to the eigenvalue of 1 is the accompanying Euler axis, since the axis is the only (nonzero) vector which remains unchanged by left-multiplying (rotating) it with the rotation matrix.

The above properties are equivalent to
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 |\hat{\mathbf u}| = |\hat{\mathbf v}| = |\hat{\mathbf w}| &= 1\\
 \hat{\mathbf u} \cdot \hat{\mathbf v} &= 0\\
 \hat{\mathbf u} \times \hat{\mathbf v} &= \hat{\mathbf w} \,,
\end{align}</math>
which is another way of stating that {{math|('''û''', '''v̂''', '''ŵ''')}} form a 3D [[orthonormal basis]]. These statements comprise a total of 6 conditions (the cross product contains 3), leaving the rotation matrix with just 3 degrees of freedom, as required.

Two successive rotations represented by matrices {{math|'''A'''<sub>1</sub>}} and {{math|'''A'''<sub>2</sub>}} are easily combined as elements of a group,
<math display="block">\mathbf{A}_\text{total} = \mathbf{A}_2\mathbf{A}_1</math> 
(Note the order, since the vector being rotated is multiplied from the right).

The ease by which vectors can be rotated using a rotation matrix, as well as the ease of combining successive rotations, make the rotation matrix a useful and popular way to represent rotations, even though it is less concise than other representations.

===Euler axis and angle (rotation vector)===
[[Image:Euler AxisAngle.png|thumb|right|A visualization of a rotation represented by an Euler axis and angle.]]
{{Main article|Axis–angle representation}}
From [[Euler's rotation theorem]] we know that any rotation can be expressed as a single rotation about some axis. The axis is the unit vector (unique except for sign) which remains unchanged by the rotation. The magnitude of the angle is also unique, with its sign being determined by the sign of the rotation axis.

The axis can be represented as a three-dimensional [[unit vector]]
<math display="block">\hat{\mathbf{e}} = \begin{bmatrix} e_x \\ e_y \\ e_z \end{bmatrix}</math>
and the angle by a scalar {{mvar|θ}}.

Since the axis is normalized, it has only two [[Degrees of freedom (mechanics)|degrees of freedom]]. The angle adds the third degree of freedom to this rotation representation.

One may wish to express rotation as a ''[[rotation vector]]'', or ''Euler vector'', an un-normalized three-dimensional vector the direction of which specifies the axis, and the length of which is {{mvar|θ}},
<math display="block">\mathbf{r} = \theta \hat{\mathbf{e}}\,.</math>

The rotation vector is useful in some contexts, as it represents a three-dimensional rotation with only three [[scalar (mathematics)|scalar]] values (its components), representing the three degrees of freedom. This is also true for representations based on sequences of three Euler angles (see below).

If the rotation angle {{mvar|θ}} is zero, the axis is not uniquely defined. Combining two successive rotations, each represented by an Euler axis and angle, is not straightforward, and in fact does not satisfy the law of vector addition, which shows that finite rotations are not really vectors at all. It is best to employ the rotation matrix or quaternion notation, calculate the product, and then convert back to Euler axis and angle.

===Euler rotations===
[[Image:Praezession.svg|thumb|170px|Euler rotations of the Earth. [[Earth's rotation|Intrinsic]] (green), [[Axial precession|precession]] (blue) and [[nutation]] (red)]]
{{Main article|Euler rotations}}
The idea behind Euler rotations is to split the complete rotation of the coordinate system into three simpler constitutive rotations, called [[precession]], [[nutation]], and [[rotation|intrinsic rotation]], being each one of them an increment on one of the [[Euler angles]]. Notice that the outer matrix will represent a rotation around one of the axes of the reference frame, and the inner matrix represents a rotation around one of the moving frame axes. The middle matrix represents a rotation around an intermediate axis called '''line of nodes'''.

However, the definition of Euler angles is not unique and in the literature many different conventions are used. These conventions depend on the axes about which the rotations are carried out, and their sequence (since rotations on a sphere are [[non-commutative]]).

The convention being used is usually indicated by specifying the axes about which the consecutive rotations (before being composed) take place, referring to them by index {{nowrap|(1, 2, 3)}} or letter {{nowrap|(X, Y, Z)}}. The engineering and robotics communities typically use 3-1-3 Euler angles. Notice that after composing the independent rotations, they do not rotate about their axis anymore. The most external matrix rotates the other two, leaving the second rotation matrix over the line of nodes, and the third one in a frame comoving with the body. There are {{nowrap|1=3 × 3 × 3 = 27}} possible combinations of three basic rotations but only {{nowrap|1=3 × 2 × 2 = 12}} of them can be used for representing arbitrary 3D rotations as Euler angles. These 12&nbsp;combinations avoid consecutive rotations around the same axis (such as XXY) which would reduce the degrees of freedom that can be represented.

Therefore, Euler angles are never expressed in terms of the external frame, or in terms of the co-moving rotated body frame, but in a mixture. Other conventions (e.g., [[rotation matrix]] or [[Quaternions and spatial rotation|quaternions]]) are used to avoid this problem.

In [[aviation]] orientation of the aircraft is usually expressed as [[Euler angles#Intrinsic rotations|intrinsic]] [[Euler angles#Tait.E2.80.93Bryan angles|Tait-Bryan angles]] following the {{math|''z''-''y''′-''x''″}} convention, which are called [[Course (navigation)#Aircraft heading|'''''heading''''']], [[Elevation (ballistics)|'''''elevation''''']], and [[Banked turn|'''''bank''''']] (or synonymously, [[Yaw (rotation)|'''''yaw''''']], [[Pitching moment|'''''pitch''''']], and '''''roll''''').

===Quaternions===
{{Main article|Quaternions and spatial rotation}}

[[Quaternion]]s, which form a four-dimensional [[vector space]], have proven very useful in representing rotations due to several advantages over the other representations mentioned in this article.

A quaternion representation of rotation is written as a [[versor]] (normalized quaternion):
<math display="block">\hat{\mathbf{q}} =q_i\mathbf{i}+q_j\mathbf{j}+q_k\mathbf{k}+q_r = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \\ q_r \end{bmatrix}</math>

The above definition stores the quaternion as an array following the convention used in (Wertz 1980) and (Markley 2003). An alternative definition, used for example in (Coutsias 1999) and (Schmidt 2001), defines the "scalar" term as the first quaternion element, with the other elements shifted down one position.

In terms of the Euler axis 
<math display="block">\hat{\mathbf{e}} = \begin{bmatrix} e_x \\ e_y \\ e_z \end{bmatrix}</math>

and angle {{mvar|θ}} this versor's components are expressed as follows: 
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 q_i &= e_x\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\
 q_j &= e_y\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\
 q_k &= e_z\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\
 q_r &= \cos\frac{\theta}{2}
\end{align}</math>

Inspection shows that the quaternion parametrization obeys the following constraint:
<math display="block">q_i^2 + q_j^2 + q_k^2 + q_r^2 = 1</math>

The last term (in our definition) is often called the scalar term, which has its origin in quaternions when understood as the mathematical extension of the complex numbers, written as 
<math display="block">a + b i + c j + d k \qquad \text{with } a, b, c, d \in \R</math>
and where {{math|{''i'', ''j'', ''k''}<nowiki/>}} are the [[hypercomplex number]]s satisfying
<math display="block">
\begin{array}{ccccccc}
 i^2 &=& j^2 &=& k^2 &=& -1\\
  ij &=& -ji &=& k&&\\
  jk &=& -kj &=& i&&\\
  ki &=& -ik &=& j&&
\end{array}
</math>

Quaternion multiplication, which is used to specify a [[function composition|composite]] rotation, is performed in the same manner as multiplication of [[complex numbers]], except that the order of the elements must be taken into account, since multiplication is not commutative. In matrix notation we can write quaternion multiplication as
<math display="block">
\tilde{\mathbf{q}}\otimes\mathbf{q} =
\begin{bmatrix}
   \;\;\, q_r & \;\;\, q_k & -q_j & \;\;\, q_i\\
   -q_k & \;\;\, q_r & \;\;\, q_i & \;\;\, q_j\\
   \;\;\, q_j & -q_i & \;\;\, q_r & \;\;\, q_k\\
   -q_i & -q_j & -q_k & \;\;\, q_r
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
   \tilde{q}_i\\
   \tilde{q}_j\\
   \tilde{q}_k\\
   \tilde{q}_r
\end{bmatrix} =
\begin{bmatrix}
   \;\;\, \tilde{q}_r & -\tilde{q}_k & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_j & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_i\\
   \;\;\, \tilde{q}_k & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_r & -\tilde{q}_i & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_j\\
   -\tilde{q}_j & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_i & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_r & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_k\\
   -\tilde{q}_i & -\tilde{q}_j & -\tilde{q}_k & \;\;\, \tilde{q}_r
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
   q_i\\
   q_j\\
   q_k\\
   q_r
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

Combining two consecutive quaternion rotations is therefore just as simple as using the rotation matrix. Just as two successive rotation matrices, {{math|'''A'''<sub>1</sub>}} followed by {{math|'''A'''<sub>2</sub>}}, are combined as
<math display="block">\mathbf{A}_3 = \mathbf{A}_2\mathbf{A}_1,</math>
we can represent this with quaternion parameters in a similarly concise way:
<math display="block">\mathbf{q}_3 = \mathbf{q}_2 \otimes \mathbf{q}_1</math>

Quaternions are a very popular parametrization due to the following properties:
*More compact than the matrix representation and less susceptible to [[round-off error]]s
*Expression of the rotation matrix in terms of quaternion parameters involves no [[trigonometric function]]s
*It is simple to combine two individual rotations represented as quaternions using a quaternion product

Like rotation matrices, quaternions must sometimes be renormalized due to rounding errors, to make sure that they correspond to valid rotations. The computational cost of renormalizing a quaternion, however, is much less than for normalizing a {{nowrap|3 × 3}} matrix.

Quaternions also capture the spinorial character of rotations in three dimensions. For a three-dimensional object connected to its (fixed) surroundings by slack strings or bands, the strings or bands can be untangled after ''two'' complete turns about some fixed axis from an initial untangled state. Algebraically, the quaternion describing such a rotation changes from a scalar +1 (initially), through (scalar + pseudovector) values to scalar −1 (at one full turn), through (scalar + pseudovector) values back to scalar +1 (at two full turns). This cycle repeats every 2 turns. After {{math|2''n''}} turns (integer {{math|''n'' > 0}}), without any intermediate untangling attempts, the strings/bands can be partially untangled back to the {{math|2(''n'' − 1)}} turns state with each application of the same procedure used in untangling from 2 turns to 0 turns. Applying the same procedure {{math|''n''}} times will take a {{math|2''n''}}-tangled object back to the untangled or 0 turn state. The untangling process also removes any rotation-generated twisting about the strings/bands themselves. Simple 3D mechanical models can be used to demonstrate these facts.

=== Rodrigues vector ===
{{See also|Rodrigues' rotation formula}}
The '''Rodrigues vector''' (sometimes called the '''Gibbs vector''', with coordinates called '''Rodrigues parameters''')<ref name=Rodrigues>{{cite journal | last1 = Rodrigues | first1 = Olinde | author-link = Olinde Rodrigues | year = 1840 | title = Des lois géometriques qui regissent les déplacements d'un systéme solide dans l'espace, et de la variation des coordonnées provenant de ces déplacement considérées indépendant des causes qui peuvent les produire | journal = J. Math. Pures Appl. | volume = 5 | pages = 380–440 }} [http://sites.mathdoc.fr/JMPA/PDF/JMPA_1840_1_5_A39_0.pdf online]</ref><ref>cf. J Willard Gibbs (1884). ''Elements of Vector Analysis'', New Haven,  p. 67</ref> can be expressed in terms of the axis and angle of the rotation as follows:
<math display="block">\mathbf{g} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}\tan\frac{\theta}{2}</math>

This representation is a higher-dimensional analog of the [[gnomonic projection]], mapping unit quaternions from a 3-sphere onto the 3-dimensional pure-vector [[hyperplane]].

It has a discontinuity at 180° ({{pi}} radians): as any rotation vector {{math|'''r'''}} tends to an angle of {{pi}} radians, its tangent tends to infinity.

A rotation {{math|'''g'''}} followed by a rotation {{math|'''f'''}} in the Rodrigues representation has the simple rotation composition form
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation =  
<math>(\mathbf{g},\mathbf{f}) = \frac{\mathbf{g}+\mathbf{f}-\mathbf{f}\times\mathbf{g}}{1-\mathbf{g}\cdot\mathbf{f}} \,.</math>
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0070BF
|bgcolor=#FAFFFB}}
Today, the most straightforward way to prove this formula is in the (faithful) [[Pauli matrices#SU(2)|doublet representation]], where {{math|1='''g''' = '''n̂''' tan ''a''}}, etc.

The combinatoric features of the Pauli matrix derivation just mentioned are also identical to the equivalent  [[quaternion]] derivation below.  Construct a quaternion associated with a spatial rotation {{mvar|R}} as,
<math display="block"> S = \cos\frac{\phi}{2} + \sin\frac{\phi}{2} \mathbf{S}. </math>
Then the composition of the rotation {{mvar|R<sub>B</sub>}} with {{mvar|R<sub>A</sub>}} is the rotation {{math|''R<sub>C</sub>'' {{=}} ''R<sub>B</sub>R<sub>A</sub>''}}, with rotation axis and angle defined by the product of the quaternions,
<math display="block">A=\cos\frac{\alpha}{2}+ \sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\mathbf{A}\quad
\text{and} \quad B=\cos\frac{\beta}{2}+ \sin\frac{\beta}{2}\mathbf{B},</math>
that is
<math display="block"> C  = \cos\frac{\gamma}{2}+\sin\frac{\gamma}{2}\mathbf{C}
=
\left(\cos\frac{\beta}{2}+\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\mathbf{B}\right) \left(\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} + \sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\mathbf{A}\right).
</math>

Expand this quaternion product to  
<math display="block">
\cos\frac{\gamma}{2}+\sin\frac{\gamma}{2} \mathbf{C}  =
\left(\cos\frac{\beta}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} - 
\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{B}\cdot \mathbf{A}\right) +  \left(\sin\frac{\beta}{2} \cos\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{B} + 
\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} \cos\frac{\beta}{2} \mathbf{A} + 
\sin\frac{\beta}{2} \sin\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{B}\times \mathbf{A}\right).
</math>

Divide both sides of this equation by the identity resulting from the previous one,
<math display="block"> \cos\frac{\gamma}{2} = \cos\frac{\beta}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} - 
\sin\frac{\beta}{2}\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{B}\cdot \mathbf{A},</math>
and evaluate
{{Equation box 1
|indent =:
|equation = <math> \tan\frac{\gamma}{2} \mathbf{C} = \frac{\tan\frac{\beta}{2}\mathbf{B} + 
\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{A} + 
\tan\frac{\beta}{2}\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{B}\times \mathbf{A}}{1 - 
\tan\frac{\beta}{2}\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} \mathbf{B}\cdot \mathbf{A}}.
</math>
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0070BF
|bgcolor=#FAFFFB}}

This is Rodrigues' formula for the axis of a composite rotation defined in terms of the axes of the two component rotations.  He derived this formula in 1840 (see page 408).<ref name=Rodrigues />   The three rotation axes {{math|'''A'''}}, {{math|'''B'''}}, and {{math|'''C'''}} form a spherical triangle and the dihedral angles between the planes formed by the sides of this triangle are defined by the rotation angles.

=== Conformal rotation vector ===
{{main|Conformal rotation vector}}

The [[stereographic projection]] of a unit quaternion onto the pure-imaginary hyperplane is called the [[conformal rotation vector]], with coordinates sometimes called ''Modified Rodrigues parameters'' (MRPs).

The conformal rotation vector can be expressed in terms of Euler axis and angle by
<math display="block">\mathbf{p} = \hat{\mathbf{e}}\tan\frac{\theta}{4}\,.</math>
The MRPs can be expressed in terms of the components of a unit quaternion representing the same rotation as
<math display="block">p_{x,y,z} = \frac{q_{i,j,k}}{1 + q_r}\,.</math>

The stereographic projection of the opposite quaternion {{math|−'''q'''}} results in a different conformal rotation vector {{math|'''p'''<sup>''s''</sup>}} than the projection of the original quaternion {{math|'''q'''}}.  Comparing components one obtains that
<math display="block">p^s_{x,y,z} = \frac{-q_{i,j,k}}{1-q_r} =\frac{-p_{x,y,z}}{\mathbf{p}^2}\,.</math>
Notably, if one of these vectors lies inside the unit 3-sphere, the other will lie outside.

Using the same notation as above, a unit quaternion is obtained with:

<math>
s = \frac{2}{1 + \lVert \mathbf{p} \rVert^2},\qquad
\begin{cases}
q_r &= s-1,\\
q_i &= s\,p_x,\\
q_j &= s\,p_y,\\
q_k &= s\,p_z.
\end{cases}
</math>

===Higher-dimensional analogues===
{{See also|Rotations in 4-dimensional Euclidean space}}

=== Vector transformation law ===
Active rotations of a 3D vector {{math|'''p'''}} in Euclidean space around an axis {{math|'''n'''}} over an angle {{math|''η''}} can be easily written in terms of dot and cross products as follows:

<math display="block">\mathbf{p}' = p_\parallel \mathbf{n} + \cos{\eta} \, \mathbf{p}_\perp + \sin{\eta} \, \mathbf{p} \wedge \mathbf{n}</math>
wherein
<math display="block">p_\parallel = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}</math>
is the longitudinal component of {{math|'''p'''}} along {{math|'''n'''}}, given by the [[dot product]],
<math display="block">\mathbf{p}_\perp = \mathbf{p} - (\mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{n}</math> 
is the transverse component of {{math|'''p'''}} with respect to {{math|'''n'''}}, and
<math display="block">\mathbf{p} \wedge \mathbf{n}</math>

is the [[cross product]] of {{math|'''p'''}} with {{math|'''n'''}}.

The above formula shows that the longitudinal component of {{math|'''p'''}} remains unchanged, whereas the transverse portion of {{math|'''p'''}} is rotated in the plane perpendicular to {{math|'''n'''}}. This plane is spanned by the transverse portion of {{math|'''p'''}} itself and a direction perpendicular to both {{math|'''p'''}} and {{math|'''n'''}}. The rotation is directly identifiable in the equation as a 2D rotation over an angle {{math|''η''}}.

Passive rotations can be described by the same formula, but with an inverse sign of either {{math|''η''}} or {{math|'''n'''}}.

==Conversions==
{{further|Charts on SO(3)}}

===Rotation matrix ↔ Euler angles===
The Euler angles {{math|(''φ'', ''θ'', ''ψ'')}} can be extracted from the rotation matrix {{math|'''A'''}} by inspecting the rotation matrix in analytical form.

====Rotation matrix → Euler angles ({{math|''z''-''x''-''z''}} extrinsic) ====
Using the {{mvar|x}}-convention, the 3-1-3 [[Euler angles#Extrinsic rotations|extrinsic]] Euler angles {{mvar|φ}}, {{mvar|θ}} and {{mvar|ψ}} (around the {{mvar|z}}-axis, {{mvar|x}}-axis and again the <math> Z</math>-axis) can be obtained as follows:
<math display="block">
\begin{align} 
 \phi   &=  \operatorname{atan2}\left(A_{31}, A_{32}\right)\\
 \theta &=  \arccos\left(A_{33}\right)\\
 \psi   &= -\operatorname{atan2}\left(A_{13}, A_{23}\right)
\end{align}
</math>

Note that {{math|atan2(''a'', ''b'')}} is equivalent to {{math|arctan {{sfrac|''a''|''b''}}}} where it also takes into account the [[Cartesian coordinate system#Cartesian coordinates in two dimensions|quadrant]] that the point {{math|(''b'', ''a'')}} is in; see [[atan2]].

When implementing the conversion, one has to take into account several situations:<ref>[http://cmp.felk.cvut.cz/cmp/courses/ROB/roblec/serial-noteeng.pdf Direct and inverse kinematics] lecture notes, page 5</ref>
* There are generally two solutions in the interval {{math|[−''π'', ''π'']<sup>3</sup>}}. The above formula works only when {{math|θ}} is within the interval {{math|[0, ''π'']}}.
* For the special case {{math|1=''A''<sub>33</sub> = 0}}, {{mvar|φ}} and {{mvar|ψ}} will be derived from {{math|''A''<sub>11</sub>}} and {{math|''A''<sub>12</sub>}}.
* There are infinitely many but countably many solutions outside of the interval {{math|[−''π'', ''π'']<sup>3</sup>}}.
* Whether all mathematical solutions apply for a given application depends on the situation.

==== Euler angles ({{math|''z''-''y''′-''x''″}} intrinsic) → rotation matrix ====
{{main|Davenport chained rotations#Tait–Bryan chained rotations}}
The rotation matrix {{math|'''A'''}} is generated from the 3-2-1 [[Euler angles#Intrinsic rotations|intrinsic]] Euler angles by multiplying the three matrices generated by rotations about the axes. 
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{A}_3\mathbf{A}_2\mathbf{A}_1 = \mathbf{A}_Z\mathbf{A}_Y\mathbf{A}_X</math>

The axes of the rotation depend on the specific convention being used. For the {{mvar|x}}-convention the rotations are about the {{mvar|x}}-, {{mvar|y}}- and {{mvar|z}}-axes with angles {{mvar|ϕ}}, {{mvar|θ}} and {{mvar|ψ}}, the individual matrices are as follows:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \mathbf{A}_X &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0\\ 0 & \cos\phi & -\sin\phi\\ 0 & \sin\phi & \cos\phi \end{bmatrix} \\[5px]
 \mathbf{A}_Y &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & 0 & \sin\theta\\ 0 & 1 & 0\\ -\sin\theta & 0 & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} \\[5px]
 \mathbf{A}_Z &= \begin{bmatrix} \cos\psi & -\sin\psi & 0\\ \sin\psi & \cos\psi & 0\\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
\end{align}</math>

This yields
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}
  \cos\theta \cos\psi &  -\cos\phi \sin\psi + \sin\phi \sin\theta \cos\psi &   \sin\phi \sin\psi + \cos\phi \sin\theta \cos\psi \\
  \cos\theta\sin\psi &  \cos\phi \cos\psi + \sin\phi \sin\theta \sin\psi &  - \sin\phi \cos\psi + \cos\phi \sin\theta \sin\psi \\
  -\sin\theta             &  \sin\phi \cos\theta                                          &   \cos\phi \cos\theta \\
 \end{bmatrix}</math>
Note: This is valid for a [[Right-hand rule|right-hand]] system, which is the convention used in almost all engineering and physics disciplines.

The interpretation of these right-handed rotation matrices is that they express coordinate transformations ([[Active and passive transformation#Passive transformation|passive]]) as opposed to point transformations ([[Active and passive transformation#Passive transformation|active]]). Because {{math|'''A'''}} expresses a rotation from the local frame {{math|'''1'''}} to the global frame {{math|'''0'''}} (i.e., {{math|'''A'''}} encodes the axes of frame {{math|'''1'''}} with respect to frame {{math|'''0'''}}), the elementary rotation matrices are composed as above. Because the inverse rotation is just the rotation transposed, if we wanted the global-to-local rotation from frame {{math|'''0'''}} to frame {{math|'''1'''}}, we would write
<math display="block">\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T} = (\mathbf{A}_Z\mathbf{A}_Y\mathbf{A}_X)^\mathsf{T} = \mathbf{A}_X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}_Y^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{A}_Z^\mathsf{T}\,.</math>

===Rotation matrix ↔ Euler axis/angle===

If the Euler angle {{mvar|θ}} is not a multiple of {{pi}}, the Euler axis {{math|'''ê'''}} and angle {{mvar|θ}} can be computed from the elements of the rotation matrix {{math|A}} as follows:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \theta &= \arccos\frac{A_{11}+A_{22}+A_{33}-1}{2}\\
    e_1 &= \frac{A_{32}-A_{23}}{2\sin\theta}\\
    e_2 &= \frac{A_{13}-A_{31}}{2\sin\theta}\\
    e_3 &= \frac{A_{21}-A_{12}}{2\sin\theta}
\end{align}</math>

Alternatively, the following method can be used:

Eigendecomposition of the rotation matrix yields the eigenvalues 1 and {{math|cos ''θ'' ± ''i'' sin ''θ''}}. The Euler axis is the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue of 1, and {{mvar|θ}} can be computed from the remaining eigenvalues.

The Euler axis can be also found using singular value decomposition since it is the normalized vector spanning the null-space of the matrix {{math|'''I''' − '''A'''}}.

To convert the other way the rotation matrix corresponding to an Euler axis {{math|'''ê'''}} and angle {{mvar|θ}} can be computed according to [[Rodrigues' rotation formula]] (with appropriate modification<!-- the article referenced describes an active rotation whereas this article describes a passive rotation, thus the sign difference -->) as follows:
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{I}_3\cos\theta + (1-\cos\theta)\hat{\mathbf{e}}\hat{\mathbf{e}}^\mathsf{T} + \left[\hat{\mathbf{e}}\right]_{\times} \sin\theta</math>

with {{math|'''I'''<sub>3</sub>}} the {{nowrap|3 × 3}} [[identity matrix]], and
<math display="block">\left[\hat{\mathbf{e}}\right]_{\times} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -e_3 & e_2\\ e_3 & 0 & -e_1\\ -e_2 & e_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} </math>

is the [[Cross product#Conversion to matrix multiplication|cross-product matrix]].

This expands to:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
A_{11} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_1^2 + \cos\theta \\
A_{12} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_1 e_2 - e_3 \sin\theta \\
A_{13} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_1 e_3 + e_2 \sin\theta \\
A_{21} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_2 e_1 + e_3 \sin\theta \\
A_{22} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_2^2 + \cos\theta \\
A_{23} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_2 e_3 - e_1 \sin\theta \\
A_{31} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_3 e_1 - e_2 \sin\theta \\
A_{32} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_3 e_2 + e_1 \sin\theta \\
A_{33} &= (1-\cos\theta) e_3^2 + \cos\theta
\end{align}</math>

{{see also|Rotation matrix#Rotation matrix from axis and angle}}

===Rotation matrix ↔ quaternion===
When computing a quaternion from the rotation matrix there is a sign ambiguity, since {{math|'''q'''}} and {{math|−'''q'''}} represent the same rotation.

One way of computing the quaternion
<math display="block">\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \\ q_r \end{bmatrix} = q_i\mathbf{i}+q_j\mathbf{j}+q_k\mathbf{k}+q_r</math>
from the rotation matrix {{math|'''A'''}} is as follows:
<math display="block">\begin{align} 
 q_r &= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1+A_{11}+A_{22}+A_{33}}\\
 q_i &= \frac{1}{4q_r}\left(A_{32}- A_{23}\right)\\
 q_j &= \frac{1}{4q_r}\left(A_{13}- A_{31}\right)\\
 q_k &= \frac{1}{4q_r}\left(A_{21}- A_{12}\right)
\end{align}</math>

There are three other mathematically equivalent ways to compute {{math|'''q'''}}. Numerical inaccuracy can be reduced by avoiding situations in which the denominator is close to zero. One of the other three methods looks as follows:<ref>{{cite arXiv|last = Mebius | first = Johan|eprint = math/0701759|title = Derivation of the Euler–Rodrigues formula for three-dimensional rotations from the general formula for four-dimensional rotations| year = 2007}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Shuster |first1=Malcolm D. |title=A Survey of Attitude Representations |journal=Journal of the Astronautical Sciences |volume=41 |issue=4 |date=1993 |pages=439–517 |bibcode=<!-- useless bibcode 1993JAnSc..41..439S --> |url=http://malcolmdshuster.com/Pub_1993h_J_Repsurv_scan.pdf }}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align} 
 q_i &= \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{1 + A_{11} - A_{22} - A_{33}}\\
 q_j &= \frac{1}{4q_i}\left(A_{12} + A_{21}\right)\\
 q_k &= \frac{1}{4q_i}\left(A_{13} + A_{31}\right)\\
 q_r &= \frac{1}{4q_i}\left(A_{32} - A_{23}\right)
\end{align}</math>

The rotation matrix corresponding to the quaternion {{math|'''q'''}} can be computed as follows:
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \left(q_r^2 - \check{\mathbf{q}}^\mathsf{T}\check{\mathbf{q}}\right)\mathbf{I}_3 + 2\check{\mathbf{q}}\check{\mathbf{q}}^\mathsf{T} + 2q_r\mathbf{\mathcal{Q}}</math>
where
<math display="block">\check{\mathbf{q}} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i\\q_j\\q_k\end{bmatrix} \,, \quad \mathbf{\mathcal{Q}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -q_k & q_j\\ q_k & 0 & -q_i\\ -q_j & q_i & 0 \end{bmatrix}</math>
which gives
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}
 1 - 2q_j^2 - 2q_k^2 & 2\left(q_iq_j - q_kq_r\right)  & 2\left(q_iq_k + q_jq_r\right)\\
 2\left(q_iq_j + q_kq_r\right)  & 1 - 2q_i^2- 2 q_k^2 & 2\left(q_jq_k - q_iq_r\right)\\
 2\left(q_iq_k - q_jq_r\right)  & 2\left(q_jq_k + q_iq_r\right)  & 1 - 2q_i^2 - 2q_j^2
\end{bmatrix}</math>

or equivalently
<math display="block">\mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix}
 -1 + 2q_i^2 + 2q_r^2 & 2\left(q_iq_j - q_kq_r\right)   & 2\left(q_iq_k + q_jq_r\right)\\
 2\left(q_iq_j + q_kq_r\right)   & -1 + 2q_j^2 + 2q_r^2 & 2\left(q_jq_k - q_iq_r\right)\\
 2\left(q_iq_k - q_jq_r\right)   & 2\left(q_jq_k + q_iq_r\right)   & -1 + 2q_k^2 + 2q_r^2
\end{bmatrix}</math>

This is called the [[Euler–Rodrigues formula]] for the [[transformation matrix]] <math>\mathbf{A}</math>

===Euler angles ↔ quaternion===
{{main article|Conversion between quaternions and Euler angles}}

==== Euler angles ({{math|''z''-''x''-''z''}} extrinsic) → quaternion ====
We will consider the {{mvar|x}}-convention 3-1-3 [[Euler angles#Extrinsic rotations|extrinsic Euler angles]] for the following algorithm. The terms of the algorithm depend on the convention used.

We can compute the quaternion
<math display="block">\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \\ q_r \end{bmatrix} = q_i\mathbf{i}+q_j\mathbf{j}+q_k\mathbf{k}+q_r</math>
from the Euler angles {{math|(''ϕ'', ''θ'', ''ψ'')}} as follows:

<math display="block">\begin{align}
 q_i &= \cos\frac{\phi - \psi}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\
 q_j &= \sin\frac{\phi - \psi}{2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\\
 q_k &= \sin\frac{\phi + \psi}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}\\
 q_r &= \cos\frac{\phi + \psi}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}
\end{align}</math>

==== Euler angles ({{math|''z''-''y''′-''x''″}} intrinsic) → quaternion ====
A quaternion equivalent to [[Yaw (rotation)|yaw]] ({{mvar|ψ}}), [[Pitching moment|pitch]] ({{mvar|θ}}) and roll ({{mvar|ϕ}}) angles. or [[Euler angles#Intrinsic rotations|intrinsic]] [[Euler angles#Tait.E2.80.93Bryan angles|Tait–Bryan angles]] following the {{math|''z''-''y''′-''x''″}} convention, can be computed by

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
 q_i &= \sin \frac{\phi}{2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\psi}{2} -  \cos \frac{\phi}{2} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \sin \frac{\psi}{2}\\
 q_j &= \cos \frac{\phi}{2} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\psi}{2} +  \sin \frac{\phi}{2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \sin \frac{\psi}{2}\\
 q_k &= \cos \frac{\phi}{2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \sin \frac{\psi}{2} -  \sin \frac{\phi}{2} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\psi}{2}\\
 q_r &= \cos \frac{\phi}{2} \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \cos \frac{\psi}{2} +  \sin \frac{\phi}{2} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \sin \frac{\psi}{2}
\end{align}
</math>

==== Quaternion → Euler angles ({{math|''z''-''x''-''z''}} extrinsic) ====
Given the rotation quaternion
<math display="block">\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \\ q_r \end{bmatrix} = q_i\mathbf{i}+q_j\mathbf{j}+q_k\mathbf{k}+q_r \,,</math>
the {{mvar|x}}-convention 3-1-3 [[Euler angles#Extrinsic rotations|extrinsic Euler Angles]] {{math|(''φ'', ''θ'', ''ψ'')}} can be computed by

<math display="block">
\begin{align}
 \phi   &=  \operatorname{atan2}\left(\left(q_iq_k + q_jq_r\right), -\left(q_jq_k - q_iq_r\right)\right)\\
 \theta &=  \arccos\left(-q_i^2 - q_j^2 + q_k^2+q_r^2\right)\\
 \psi   &= \operatorname{atan2}\left(\left(q_iq_k - q_jq_r\right), \left(q_jq_k + q_iq_r\right)\right)
\end{align}
</math>

==== Quaternion → Euler angles ({{math|''z''-''y''′-''x''″}} intrinsic) ====
Given the rotation quaternion
<math display="block">\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \\ q_r \end{bmatrix} = q_i\mathbf{i}+q_j\mathbf{j}+q_k\mathbf{k}+q_r \,,</math>
[[Yaw (rotation)|yaw]], [[Pitching moment|pitch]] and roll angles, or [[Euler angles#Intrinsic rotations|intrinsic]] [[Euler angles#Tait.E2.80.93Bryan angles|Tait–Bryan angles]] following the {{math|''z''-''y''′-''x''″}} convention, can be computed by

<math display="block">\begin{align}
\text{roll}   &= \operatorname{atan2} \left(2\left(q_r q_i + q_j q_k\right),1 - 2\left(q_i^2 + q_j^2\right)\right) \\
\text{pitch} &= \arcsin \left(2\left(q_r q_j - q_k q_i\right)\right) \\
\text{yaw}  &= \operatorname{atan2} \left(2\left(q_r q_k + q_i q_j\right),1 - 2\left(q_j^2 + q_k^2\right)\right)
\end{align} </math>

===Euler axis–angle ↔ quaternion===
Given the Euler axis {{math|'''ê'''}} and angle {{mvar|θ}}, the quaternion
<math display="block">\mathbf{q} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \\ q_r \end{bmatrix} = q_i\mathbf{i}+q_j\mathbf{j}+q_k\mathbf{k}+q_r \,,</math>

can be computed by
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 q_i &= \hat{e}_1\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \\
 q_j &= \hat{e}_2\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \\
 q_k &= \hat{e}_3\sin\frac{\theta}{2} \\
 q_r &= \cos\frac{\theta}{2}
\end{align}</math>

Given the rotation quaternion {{math|'''q'''}}, define
<math display="block">\check{\mathbf{q}} = \begin{bmatrix} q_i \\ q_j \\ q_k \end{bmatrix}\,.</math>
Then the Euler axis {{math|'''ê'''}} and angle {{mvar|θ}} can be computed by
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \hat{\mathbf{e}} &= \frac{\check{\mathbf{q}}}{\left\|\check{\mathbf{q}}\right\|} \\
 \theta &= 2\arccos q_r
\end{align}</math>

=== Rotation matrix ↔ Rodrigues vector ===

==== Rodrigues vector → Rotation matrix ====

Since the definition of the Rodrigues vector can be related to rotation quaternions:<math display="block">
\begin{cases}
    g_i = \dfrac{q_i}{q_r} = e_x \tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right) \\
    g_j = \dfrac{q_j}{q_r} = e_y \tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)\\
    g_k = \dfrac{q_k}{q_r} = e_z \tan\left(\dfrac{\theta}{2}\right)
\end{cases}</math>By making use of the following property<math display="block">
1 = q_r^2 + q_i^2 + q_j^2 + q_k^2 = q_r^2 \left(1 + \frac{q_i^2}{q_r^2} + \frac{q_j^2}{q_r^2} + \frac{q_k^2}{q_r^2}\right) = q_r^2 \left(1 + g_i^2 + g_j^2 + g_k^2\right)</math>The formula can be obtained by factoring {{math|''q''{{su|b=''r''|p=2}}}} from the final expression obtained for quaternions:

<math>\mathbf{A} = q_r^2 \begin{bmatrix}
 \frac{1}{q_r^2} - 2\frac{q_j^2}{q_r^2} - 2\frac{q_k^2}{q_r^2} & 2\left(\frac{q_i}{q_r}\frac{q_j}{q_r} - \frac{q_k}{q_r}\right)  & 2\left(\frac{q_i}{q_r}\frac{q_k}{q_r} + \frac{q_j}{q_r}\right)\\
 2\left(\frac{q_i}{q_r}\frac{q_j}{q_r} + \frac{q_k}{q_r}\right)  & \frac{1}{q_r^2} - 2\frac{q_i^2}{q_r^2} - 2 \frac{q_k^2}{q_r^2} & 2\left(\frac{q_j}{q_r}\frac{q_k}{q_r} - \frac{q_i}{q_r}\right)\\
 2\left(\frac{q_i}{q_r}\frac{q_k}{q_r} - \frac{q_j}{q_r}\right)  & 2\left(\frac{q_j}{q_r}\frac{q_k}{q_r} + \frac{q_i}{q_r}\right)  & \frac{1}{q_r^2} - 2\frac{q_i^2}{q_r^2} - 2\frac{q_j^2}{q_r^2}
\end{bmatrix}</math>

Leading to the final formula:

<math>\mathbf{A} = \frac{1}{1+g_i^2+g_j^2+g_k^2} \begin{bmatrix}
 1 + g_i^2 - g_j^2 - g_k^2 & 2\left(g_i g_j - g_k\right)  & 2\left(g_i g_k + g_j\right)\\
 2\left(g_i g_j + g_k\right)  &1 - g_i^2 + g_j^2 - g_k^2 & 2\left(g_j g_k - g_i\right)\\
 2\left(g_i g_k - g_j\right)  & 2\left(g_j g_k + g_i\right)  &1 - g_i^2 - g_j^2 + g_k^2
\end{bmatrix}</math>

==Conversion formulae for derivatives==

===Rotation matrix ↔ angular velocities===
The angular velocity vector
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{\omega} = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_x \\ \omega_y \\ \omega_z \end{bmatrix}</math>
can be extracted from the [[time derivative]] of the rotation matrix {{math|{{sfrac|d'''A'''|d''t''}}}} by the following relation:
<math display="block">[\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_z & \omega_y \\ \omega_z & 0 & -\omega_x \\ -\omega_y & \omega_x & 0 \end{bmatrix}  = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}}{\mathrm{d}t}\mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}</math>

The derivation is adapted from Ioffe<ref>[http://www.euclideanspace.com/physics/kinematics/angularvelocity/mark.htm] Physics - Mark Ioffe - {{math|''W''(''t'')}} in terms of matrices</ref> as follows:

For any vector {{math|'''r'''<sub>0</sub>}}, consider {{math|1='''r'''(''t'') = '''A'''(''t'')'''r'''<sub>0</sub>}} and differentiate it:
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} \mathbf{r}_0 = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}(t) \mathrm{r}(t)</math>

The derivative of a vector is the [[Velocity vector|linear velocity]] of its tip. Since {{math|'''A'''}} is a rotation matrix, by definition the length of {{math|'''r'''(''t'')}} is always equal to the length of {{math|'''r'''<sub>0</sub>}}, and hence it does not change with time. Thus, when {{math|'''r'''(''t'')}} rotates, its tip moves along a circle, and the linear velocity of its tip is tangential to the circle; i.e., always perpendicular to {{math|'''r'''(''t'')}}. In this specific case, the relationship between the linear velocity vector and the angular velocity vector is 
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{r}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \boldsymbol{\omega}(t)\times \mathbf{r}(t) = [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times \mathbf{r}(t)</math>
(see [[circular motion]] and [[Cross product#Conversion to matrix multiplication|cross product]]).

By the [[transitive relation|transitivity]] of the abovementioned equations,  
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}(t) \mathbf{r}(t) = [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times \mathbf{r}(t)</math>

which implies
<math display="block">\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} \mathbf{A}^\mathsf{T}(t) = [\boldsymbol{\omega}]_\times</math>

===Quaternion ↔ angular velocities===
The angular velocity vector
<math display="block">\boldsymbol{\omega} = \begin{bmatrix} \omega_x \\ \omega_y \\ \omega_z \end{bmatrix}</math>
can be obtained from the derivative of the quaternion {{math|{{sfrac|d'''q'''|d''t''}}}} as follows:<ref>[http://web.cs.iastate.edu/~cs577/handouts/quaternion.pdf Quaternions and Rotation] lecture notes, p. 14-15</ref>
<math display="block"> \begin{bmatrix}
   0 \\
   \omega_x \\
   \omega_y \\
   \omega_z 
\end{bmatrix} = 2 \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{q}}{\mathrm{d}t}\tilde{\mathbf{q}}
</math>
where {{math|'''q̃'''}} is the conjugate (inverse) of {{math|'''q'''}}.

Conversely, the derivative of the quaternion is
<math display="block"> \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{q}}{\mathrm{d}t} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}
   0 \\
   \omega_x \\
   \omega_y \\
   \omega_z
\end{bmatrix}\mathbf{q} \,.
</math>

==Rotors in a geometric algebra==
The formulations of [[geometric algebra]] (GA) provides an extension and interpretation of the quaternion method. Central to GA is the geometric product of vectors, an extension of the traditional [[inner product|inner]] and [[cross product]]s, given by
<math display="block">\mathbf{ab} = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{a} \wedge \mathbf{b}</math>

where the symbol {{math|∧}} denotes the [[exterior algebra|exterior product or wedge product]]. This product of vectors {{math|'''a'''}}, and {{math|'''b'''}} produces two terms: a scalar part from the inner product and a [[bivector]] part from the wedge product. This bivector describes the plane perpendicular to what the cross product of the vectors would return.

Bivectors in GA have some unusual properties compared to vectors. Under the geometric product, bivectors have a negative square: the bivector {{math|'''x̂ŷ'''}} describes the {{mvar|xy}}-plane. Its square is {{math|1=('''x̂ŷ''')<sup>2</sup> = '''x̂ŷx̂ŷ'''}}. Because the unit basis vectors are orthogonal to each other, the geometric product reduces to the antisymmetric outer product, so {{math|'''x̂'''}} and {{math|'''ŷ'''}} can be swapped freely at the cost of a factor of&nbsp;−1. The square reduces to {{math|1=−'''x̂x̂ŷŷ''' = −1}} since the basis vectors themselves square to +1.

This result holds generally for all bivectors, and as a result the bivector plays a role similar to the [[imaginary unit]]. Geometric algebra uses bivectors in its analogue to the quaternion, the ''rotor'', given by
<math display="block">\mathbf{R} = \exp\left(\frac{-\hat\mathbf{B}\theta}{2}\right) = \cos \frac{\theta}{2} - \hat\mathbf{B} \sin \frac{\theta}{2}\,,</math>
where {{math|'''B̂'''}} is a unit bivector that describes the [[plane of rotation]]. Because {{math|'''B̂'''}} squares to −1, the [[power series]] expansion of {{math|'''R'''}} generates the [[trigonometric function]]s. The rotation formula that maps a vector {{math|'''a'''}} to a rotated vector {{math|'''b'''}} is then
<math display="block">\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{R a R}^\dagger</math>
where
<math display="block">\mathbf{R}^\dagger = \exp\left(\frac{1}{2}\hat\mathbf{B} \theta\right) = \cos \frac{\theta}{2} + \hat\mathbf{B} \sin \frac{\theta}{2}</math>
is the ''reverse'' of <math>\scriptstyle R</math> (reversing the order of the vectors in <math> B</math> is equivalent to changing its sign).

'''Example.'''  A rotation about the axis
<math display="block">\hat \mathbf{v} = \frac{1}{\sqrt 3}\left(\hat \mathbf{x} + \hat \mathbf{y} + \hat \mathbf{z}\right)</math>
can be accomplished by converting {{math|'''v̂'''}} to its dual bivector,
<math display="block">\hat \mathbf{B} = \hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{y} \hat \mathbf{z} \hat \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{i} \hat \mathbf{v} \,,</math>
where {{math|1='''i''' = '''x̂ŷẑ'''}} is the unit volume element, the only trivector (pseudoscalar) in three-dimensional space. The result is
<math display="block">\hat \mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\sqrt 3}\left(\hat \mathbf{y} \hat \mathbf{z} + \hat \mathbf{z} \hat \mathbf{x} + \hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{y}\right) \,.</math>

In three-dimensional space, however, it is often simpler to leave the expression for {{math|1='''B̂''' = '''iv̂'''}}, using the fact that {{math|'''i'''}} commutes with all objects in 3D and also squares to −1. A rotation of the {{math|'''x̂'''}} vector in this plane by an angle {{mvar|θ}} is then

<math display="block">\hat \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{R} \hat \mathbf{x} \mathbf{R}^\dagger = e^{-i\hat \mathbf{v} \frac{\theta}{2}} \hat \mathbf{x} e^{i \hat \mathbf{v} \frac{\theta}{2}} = \hat \mathbf{x} \cos^2 \frac{\theta}{2} + \mathbf{i} \left(\hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{v} - \hat \mathbf{v} \hat \mathbf{x}\right) \cos \frac{\theta}{2} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} + \hat \mathbf{v} \hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{v} \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2}</math>

Recognizing that
<math display="block">\mathbf{i} (\hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{v} - \hat \mathbf{v} \hat \mathbf{x}) = 2\mathbf{i} (\hat \mathbf{x} \wedge \hat \mathbf{v})</math>
and that {{math|−'''v̂x̂v̂'''}} is the reflection of {{math|'''x̂'''}} about the plane perpendicular to  {{math|'''v̂'''}} gives a geometric interpretation to the rotation operation:  the rotation preserves the components that are parallel to  {{math|'''v̂'''}} and changes only those that are perpendicular. The terms are then computed:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
 \hat \mathbf{v} \hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{v}    &= \frac{1}{3} \left(-\hat \mathbf{x} + 2 \hat \mathbf{y} + 2 \hat \mathbf{z}\right) \\
 2\mathbf{i} \hat \mathbf{x} \wedge \hat \mathbf{v} &= 2\mathbf{i} \frac{1}{\sqrt 3} \left(\hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{y} + \hat \mathbf{x} \hat \mathbf{z}\right) = \frac{2}{\sqrt 3} \left(\hat \mathbf{y} - \hat \mathbf{z}\right)
\end{align}</math>

The result of the rotation is then
<math display="block">\hat \mathbf{x}' = \hat \mathbf{x} \left(\cos^2 \frac{\theta}{2} - \frac{1}{3} \sin^2 \frac{\theta}{2}\right) + \frac{2}{3} \hat \mathbf{y} \sin \frac{\theta}{2}  \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2} + \sqrt{3} \cos \frac{\theta}{2}\right)  + \frac{2}{3} \hat \mathbf{z} \sin \frac{\theta}{2} \left(\sin \frac{\theta}{2} - \sqrt{3} \cos \frac{\theta}{2}\right) </math>

A simple check on this result is the angle {{math|1=''θ'' = {{sfrac|2|3}}π}}. Such a rotation should map {{math|'''x̂'''}} to {{math|'''ŷ'''}}. Indeed, the rotation reduces to
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \hat \mathbf{x}' &= \hat \mathbf{x}\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{3} \frac{3}{4}\right) + \frac{2}{3} \hat \mathbf{y} \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \left(\frac{\sqrt 3}{2} + \sqrt{3}\frac{1}{2}\right) + \frac{2}{3} \hat \mathbf{z} \frac{\sqrt 3}{2} \left(\frac{\sqrt 3}{2} - \sqrt{3}\frac{1}{2}\right) \\
                   &= 0 \hat \mathbf{x} + \hat \mathbf{y} + 0 \hat \mathbf{z} = \hat \mathbf{y}
\end{align}</math>

exactly as expected. This rotation formula is valid not only for vectors but for any [[multivector]]. In addition, when Euler angles are used, the complexity of the operation is much reduced. Compounded rotations come from multiplying the rotors, so the total rotor from Euler angles is
<math display="block">\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}_{\gamma'} \mathbf{R}_{\beta'} \mathbf{R}_\alpha = \exp\left(\frac{-\mathbf{i} \hat \mathbf{z}' \gamma}{2}\right) \exp\left(\frac{-\mathbf{i} \hat \mathbf{x}' \beta}{2}\right) \exp\left(\frac{-\mathbf{i} \hat \mathbf{z} \alpha}{2}\right)</math>
but
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\hat \mathbf{x}' &= \mathbf{R}_\alpha \hat \mathbf{x} \mathbf{R}_\alpha^\dagger \quad \text{and} \\
\hat \mathbf{z}' &= \mathbf{R}_{\beta'} \hat \mathbf{z} \mathbf{R}_{\beta'}^\dagger \,.
\end{align}</math>
These rotors come back out of the exponentials like so:
<math display="block">\mathbf{R}_{\beta'} = \cos \frac{\beta}{2} - \mathbf{i} \mathbf{R}_\alpha \hat \mathbf{x} \mathbf{R}_\alpha^\dagger \sin \frac{\beta}{2} = \mathbf{R}_\alpha \mathbf{R}_\beta \mathbf{R}_\alpha^\dagger</math>
where {{math|'''R'''<sub>''β''</sub>}} refers to rotation in the original coordinates. Similarly for the {{mvar|γ}} rotation,
<math display="block">\mathbf{R}_{\gamma'} = \mathbf{R}_{\beta'} \mathbf{R}_\gamma \mathbf{R}_{\beta'}^\dagger = \mathbf{R}_\alpha \mathbf{R}_\beta \mathbf{R}_\alpha^\dagger \mathbf{R}_\gamma \mathbf{R}_\alpha \mathbf{R}_\beta^\dagger \mathbf{R}_\alpha^\dagger \,.</math>
Noting that {{math|'''R'''<sub>''γ''</sub>}} and {{math|'''R'''<sub>''α''</sub>}} commute (rotations in the same plane must commute), and the total rotor becomes
<math display="block">\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{R}_\alpha \mathbf{R}_\beta \mathbf{R}_\gamma</math>

Thus, the compounded rotations of Euler angles become a series of equivalent rotations in the original fixed frame.

While rotors in geometric algebra work almost identically to quaternions in three dimensions, the power of this formulation is its generality:  this method is appropriate and valid in spaces with any number of dimensions. In 3D, rotations have three degrees of freedom, a degree for each linearly independent plane (bivector) the rotation can take place in. It has been known that pairs of quaternions can be used to generate rotations in 4D, yielding six degrees of freedom, and the geometric algebra approach verifies this result:  in 4D, there are six linearly independent bivectors that can be used as the generators of rotations.
